subject: DRV
body: You feel tired on a motorway journey. What should you do?
options: Stop on the hard shoulder for a sleep
Leave at the next exit or services and take a proper rest
Open the window and carry on
explanation: Opening a window only helps for a very short time.

subject: DRV
body: How often does the Highway Code recommend taking a break on a long journey?
options: At least 15 minutes every two hours
explanation: Plan rest stops before you set off.

subject: DRV
body: Before pulling out from a parked position, you should
options: pull out quickly to save time
check mirrors and look over your shoulder into the blind spot
explanation: The blind spot is not covered by your mirrors.

subject: DRV
body: Before you move off, when should you use your mirrors?
options: Only after you have moved off
Before signalling and before moving off
explanation: Mirrors – signal – manoeuvre.

subject: DRV
body: Your passenger wants to chat while you approach a busy junction. You should
options: slow to walking pace in the junction
keep talking and steer with one hand
concentrate on the road and ask them to wait
explanation: Distractions increase the risk of a collision.

subject: DRV
body: Using a satnav while driving, you should
options: watch it instead of the road
set it before your journey and only glance at it when safe
explanation: If you need to change the route, stop somewhere safe.

subject: DRV
body: Which can cause dazzle from oncoming headlights to last longer?
explanation: Keep the windscreen clean inside and out.

subject: DRV
body: Approaching a bend, a car is overtaking a cyclist towards you. You should
options: speed up to get past quickly
slow down and be ready to stop
explanation: Expect the unexpected on bends.

subject: DRV
body: A driver behind you is following too closely. What should you do?
options: Increase the gap in front of you so you can brake more gently
explanation: A bigger gap ahead gives you and them more time.

subject: DRV
body: At a pedestrian crossing, a pedestrian is slow to cross. You should
explanation: Elderly and disabled people may need more time.

subject: DRV
body: When should you flash your headlights at other road users?
options: Only to let them know you are there
explanation: Never assume a flash means it is safe to go.

subject: DRV
body: A long, slow-moving vehicle is ahead on a narrow road. You should
options: flash your lights to make it pull over
stay well back and wait for a safe place to overtake
drive very close so you can see past
explanation: Being patient is part of safe driving.

subject: DRV
body: Another driver makes a mistake that affects you. You should
options: stay calm and not react aggressively
explanation: Road rage puts everyone at risk.

subject: DRV
body: Which is an example of 'tailgating'?
explanation: Tailgating is dangerous and intimidating.

subject: DRV
body: A horse rider is ahead on a country road. How should you pass?
options: At 30 mph with a 1 metre gap
Wide and slow — at no more than 10 mph and at least 2 metres away
explanation: Horses can be startled easily.

subject: DRV
body: You are in a queue of traffic and a vehicle wants to join from a side road. You should
options: let it in if it is safe and the traffic is slow
flash your lights to show annoyance
explanation: Courtesy helps traffic flow safely.

subject: DRV
body: The minimum legal tread depth for car tyres is
options: 1.6 mm across the central three-quarters, all the way round
explanation: Many experts recommend replacing tyres well before this.

subject: DRV
body: When should you check tyre pressures?
explanation: Pressures read higher when tyres are warm.

subject: DRV
body: A head restraint should be adjusted so that
options: it is as low as possible
the rigid part is at least as high as your eyes or the top of your ears and close to your head
explanation: It reduces whiplash injuries.

subject: DRV
body: Anti-lock brakes (ABS) mainly help you
options: keep steering control while braking hard
stop in a much shorter distance on every surface
explanation: Stopping distances still increase on wet or icy roads.

subject: DRV
body: A catalytic converter is fitted to reduce
explanation: It cleans exhaust emissions.

subject: DRV
body: Which driving style saves fuel?
options: Carrying a roof box all the time
Accelerating gently and planning ahead to avoid harsh braking
Revving the engine in each gear
explanation: Smooth driving is eco-driving.

subject: DRV
body: How can you reduce fuel consumption on a long journey?
options: Drive with the windows open at high speed
Remove an unused roof rack or box
Keep the air conditioning on full
explanation: Extra drag and weight use more fuel.

subject: DRV
body: When checking the engine oil level, the car should be
options: on level ground with the engine off
just after a long drive at speed
explanation: Wait for the oil to settle.

subject: DRV
body: When must a car first have an MOT in Great Britain?
options: When it is one year old
When it is three years old
When it is five years old
explanation: Then it needs one every year. In Northern Ireland it is four years.

subject: DRV
body: Coasting (driving with the clutch down or in neutral) is dangerous because
options: it reduces your control of the vehicle
explanation: You lose engine braking and steering response.

subject: DRV
body: Who is legally responsible for making sure a child under 14 wears a seat belt or suitable restraint?
options: The child's parent if they are not in the car
explanation: Passengers aged 14 and over are responsible for themselves.

subject: DRV
body: Children must use a suitable child seat until they are
options: 12 years old or 135 cm tall, whichever comes first
explanation: The seat must suit the child's weight or height.

subject: DRV
body: A rear-facing baby seat must never be used in a front seat that has
explanation: The airbag could seriously injure the baby.

subject: DRV
body: A warning light shows on the dashboard while driving. You should
options: check what it means in the vehicle handbook and act on it
ignore it until the next service
explanation: Red lights usually mean stop as soon as it is safe.

subject: DRV
body: In good, dry conditions, the gap you should leave behind the vehicle in front is at least
explanation: Pick a fixed point and count 'Only a fool breaks the two-second rule'.

subject: DRV
body: On wet roads, your gap from the vehicle in front should be at least
explanation: Stopping distances at least double in the wet.

subject: DRV
body: On icy roads, braking distances can be up to
explanation: Drive slowly and gently.

subject: DRV
body: Your car begins to aquaplane on a flooded road. What should you do?
options: Ease off the accelerator and let the car slow down
explanation: Aquaplaning means the tyres have lost contact with the road.

subject: DRV
body: The back of your car skids to the right. What should you do?
explanation: Steer gently into the skid.

subject: DRV
body: When driving in snow, you should
options: use first gear at high revs
brake hard to test the grip
follow closely to use the car's tracks
use the highest gear possible and accelerate and brake gently
explanation: Gentle inputs keep the tyres gripping.

subject: DRV
body: After driving through a flood, you should
options: drive fast to dry the engine
explanation: Wet brakes may not work properly.

subject: DRV
body: In strong winds, which road users are most likely to be affected?
options: Cyclists, motorcyclists, high-sided vehicles and caravans
explanation: Give them more room.

subject: DRV
body: Driving downhill on a long steep hill, you should
options: ride the brakes all the way
select a lower gear to use engine braking
explanation: Overusing brakes makes them fade.

subject: DRV
body: What is the typical stopping distance at 30 mph in good conditions?
explanation: Thinking distance 9 m plus braking distance 14 m.

subject: DRV
body: A ball bounces into the road ahead. What should you do?
options: Slow down and be ready to stop for a child
explanation: A child may run out after it.

subject: DRV
body: You are passing a bus that has stopped at a bus stop. You should
options: watch for pedestrians stepping out from in front of it
explanation: People often cross in front of buses.

subject: DRV
body: An ice-cream van is parked ahead. Why should you take extra care?
options: Children may run into the road
explanation: Children may be excited and not look.

subject: DRV
body: Some prescription medicines can affect your driving. What should you do?
options: Drink coffee to counter the effects
Check the leaflet or ask your doctor or pharmacist before driving
explanation: Driving while impaired by drugs is an offence.

subject: DRV
body: Why should you be careful when passing parked cars?
options: A door may open or a pedestrian may step out
explanation: Leave room for doors opening.

subject: DRV
body: A road marking says 'SLOW' ahead. You should
options: reduce speed because there is a hazard
explanation: Look for the hazard and be ready.

subject: DRV
body: You see a vehicle with flashing amber beacons on a dual carriageway. It is probably
explanation: For example a gritter or maintenance vehicle.

subject: DRV
body: Which of these may make it harder for you to see hazards at night?
explanation: Slow down or stop if you are dazzled.

subject: DRV
body: Approaching a junction where your view is restricted, you should
options: slow down and creep forward until you can see clearly
explanation: Look, assess and decide.

subject: DRV
body: After drinking alcohol the night before, you should
options: drive normally after a cold shower
be aware you may still be over the limit the next morning
explanation: Alcohol takes time to leave your body.

subject: DRV
body: When overtaking a cyclist at speeds up to 30 mph, the Highway Code advises leaving at least
explanation: Leave more room at higher speeds.

subject: DRV
body: The Highway Code's 'hierarchy of road users' means that
options: those who can cause the greatest harm have the greatest responsibility to reduce danger
cyclists must give way to everyone
explanation: Drivers have more responsibility than cyclists and pedestrians.

subject: DRV
body: You are turning into a side road and pedestrians are waiting to cross it. You should
options: turn quickly before they step out
explanation: Rule H2 of the Highway Code.

subject: DRV
body: A pedestrian has a white cane with a red band. This means they are
explanation: A plain white cane means visually impaired.

subject: DRV
body: When passing pedestrians walking in the road (for example where there is no pavement), the Highway Code advises
options: allowing at least 2 metres and passing at low speed
explanation: Rule 206.

subject: DRV
body: The 'Dutch reach' is
options: opening the car door with the hand furthest from it so you look back for cyclists
explanation: It helps prevent 'dooring' cyclists.

subject: DRV
body: Why should you look carefully for motorcyclists at junctions?
options: They must give way to you
They are small and easy to miss
explanation: 'Think bike' before pulling out.

subject: DRV
body: You see older pedestrians about to cross the road. You should
options: be patient — they may be slower and misjudge your speed
explanation: Give them time.

subject: DRV
body: A cyclist ahead is approaching a roundabout in the left lane but intends to go right. You should
options: give them plenty of room — they may stay in the left lane
explanation: Cyclists may keep left for safety.

subject: DRV
body: Near a school with 'school keep clear' zigzag markings, you must not
options: stop or park on the markings
explanation: Children need to see and be seen.

subject: DRV
body: A long vehicle is signalling left but has moved out to the right before a junction. You should
options: stay back — it needs room to turn left
explanation: Long vehicles swing wide to turn.

subject: DRV
body: Why should you take extra care near trams?
options: They cannot steer to avoid you
explanation: Trams run on fixed rails.

subject: DRV
body: In a built-up area, a bus signals to pull out from a bus stop. You should
options: give way to it if it is safe to do so
explanation: Rule 223 of the Highway Code.

subject: DRV
body: When following a large lorry, why should you keep well back?
options: To see past it and so the driver can see you in their mirrors
Because it is illegal to follow lorries
explanation: If you can't see its mirrors, the driver can't see you.

subject: DRV
body: A vehicle with a flashing green beacon is likely to be
options: a doctor on an emergency call
explanation: Give way if you can do so safely.

subject: DRV
body: Powered vehicles used by disabled people that are restricted to 8 mph on the road are
explanation: They may use dual carriageways but must show an amber light.

subject: DRV
body: Overtaking a large vehicle in wet weather, you should be aware that
options: it travels faster in the wet
explanation: Use wipers and keep a safe gap.

subject: DRV
body: When should you use fog lights?
options: When visibility is seriously reduced, generally to less than 100 metres
explanation: Switch them off when visibility improves.

subject: DRV
body: You must use headlights at night when
options: driving in a 20 mph zone with street lights only
driving on a road without street lights
explanation: Use dipped headlights in built-up areas with street lights.

subject: DRV
body: Traffic-calming measures such as speed humps are used to
explanation: Keep to a low speed over them.

subject: DRV
body: You should not overtake when approaching
options: a bend, a junction or the brow of a hill
explanation: You cannot see what is coming.

subject: DRV
body: Your car stalls on a level crossing. What should you do first?
options: Get everyone out and clear of the crossing
Wait in the car for help
Try to restart the engine repeatedly
explanation: Then use the railway phone to tell the signal operator.

subject: DRV
body: At a level crossing, the amber light comes on followed by twin flashing red lights. You must
options: carry on if no train is visible
explanation: Keep waiting if the lights keep flashing after a train passes.

subject: DRV
body: When driving in fog, you should
options: use dipped headlights and slow down
follow the tail lights in front closely
explanation: Full beam reflects off fog.

subject: DRV
body: When reversing, you should
options: look all around and mainly through the rear window
explanation: Pedestrians and children are hard to see.

subject: DRV
body: A red X is shown above your lane on a motorway. You must
explanation: Driving under a red X is an offence.

subject: DRV
body: A speed limit shown in a red circle on a motorway gantry is
explanation: Variable limits in red circles must be obeyed.

subject: DRV
body: On a motorway, the reflective studs between the hard shoulder and the left lane are
explanation: White studs mark lanes; amber marks the central reservation; green marks slip roads.

subject: DRV
body: Green reflective studs on a motorway mark
options: the edge of slip roads and lay-bys
explanation: They show where you can leave or join.

subject: DRV
body: Amber reflective studs on a motorway mark
options: the edge of the central reservation
explanation: They are on the right-hand edge of the carriageway.

subject: DRV
body: Learner car drivers may drive on a motorway only
options: with an approved driving instructor in a car with dual controls
explanation: The law changed in June 2018.

subject: DRV
body: On a motorway with three or more lanes, which vehicles may NOT use the right-hand lane (except in some circumstances)?
options: Vehicles towing trailers and goods vehicles over 7.5 tonnes
explanation: They must use the left two lanes.

subject: DRV
body: Countdown markers before a motorway exit are placed at
explanation: Each bar represents 100 yards.

subject: DRV
body: You miss your motorway exit. What should you do?
options: Do a U-turn through the central reservation
Carry on to the next exit
explanation: Never reverse on a motorway.

subject: DRV
body: Your car breaks down on a smart motorway with no hard shoulder. If possible you should
options: stop as soon as anything feels wrong
walk across the lanes to the central reservation
get to an emergency area, the next exit or services
explanation: If stuck in a live lane, switch on hazard lights and call 999.

subject: DRV
body: On a motorway, marker posts on the hard shoulder show
options: the direction to the nearest emergency telephone
explanation: Posts are every 100 metres.

subject: DRV
body: You should overtake on a motorway
options: on the right, after checking mirrors and blind spots
on the left whenever there is space
in any lane at any time
explanation: Only pass on the left if traffic in lanes is moving slowly in queues.

subject: DRV
body: Joining a motorway from a slip road, you should
options: stop at the end of the slip road
give priority to traffic already on the motorway and match its speed
explanation: Use the slip road to build up speed.

subject: DRV
body: When can you stop on the hard shoulder?
explanation: Leave at the next exit if you need to rest.

subject: DRV
body: At a roundabout, you should normally give priority to traffic
explanation: Unless signs or markings show otherwise.

subject: DRV
body: When leaving a roundabout, signal left
options: after you have left the roundabout
after you pass the exit before the one you want
explanation: This tells others where you are going.

subject: DRV
body: You may enter a yellow box junction only if
options: your exit road or lane is clear
explanation: You may wait in it when turning right if blocked only by oncoming traffic.

subject: DRV
body: You must not park within how many metres of a junction (unless in a marked bay)?
explanation: Rule 243 of the Highway Code.

subject: DRV
body: When parking at night on a road with a speed limit over 30 mph, you must
options: leave your headlights on full beam
explanation: Always park facing the direction of traffic at night.

subject: DRV
body: In a built-up area, you must not use your horn between
options: midnight and 6 am only on Sundays
11.30 pm and 7 am, unless another road user poses a danger
explanation: And never while stationary, except in danger.

subject: DRV
body: The national speed limit sign is
options: a white circle with a black diagonal stripe
a blue circle with a white arrow
explanation: The limit depends on the road and vehicle type.

subject: DRV
body: Double white lines where the line nearer to you is solid mean
options: you must not cross or straddle them, except in specific situations
explanation: Exceptions include passing a stationary vehicle or overtaking a cyclist or horse at 10 mph or less.

subject: DRV
body: Zigzag lines at a pedestrian crossing mean you must not
options: park or overtake the lead vehicle approaching the crossing
explanation: They keep the view of the crossing clear.

subject: DRV
body: Double yellow lines along the edge of the road mean
options: no waiting during the day only
explanation: Check signs for seasonal restrictions.

subject: DRV
body: You may use a bus lane
options: only outside the times shown on the signs (or not at all if no times are shown)
if you are turning left in 200 m
explanation: Signs show when the lane is in operation.

subject: DRV
body: Driving in Wales, what is the default speed limit on most restricted roads (with street lights)?
explanation: This changed in September 2023.

subject: DRV
body: At a zebra crossing, you must
options: sound your horn to warn them
give way to pedestrians who are on the crossing
overtake slow vehicles on the crossing
explanation: Look for people waiting and be ready to stop.

subject: DRV
body: At a pelican crossing, a flashing amber light means
options: give way to pedestrians on the crossing, then go if it is clear
explanation: Puffin crossings do not have a flashing amber phase.

subject: DRV
body: A toucan crossing can be used by
explanation: Pegasus crossings are for horse riders.

subject: DRV
body: Road signs in circles generally
explanation: Triangles warn; rectangles inform.

subject: DRV
body: Most triangular road signs
explanation: They have a red border.

subject: DRV
body: Blue circular signs usually
options: tell you what you must not do
tell you what you must do
explanation: For example 'turn left' or 'keep left'.

subject: DRV
body: Red circular signs usually
options: tell you what you must not do
tell you what you must do
explanation: For example 'no entry' or speed limits.

subject: DRV
body: What shape is a stop sign?
explanation: Its unique shape can be recognised even if covered in snow.

subject: DRV
body: A 'give way' sign is
explanation: Give way to traffic on the major road.

subject: DRV
body: Brown road signs show
explanation: Green backgrounds show primary routes; blue shows motorways.

subject: DRV
body: Direction signs with a blue background are used on
explanation: Primary routes use green backgrounds.

subject: DRV
body: What is the sequence of UK traffic lights after red?
explanation: Red and amber together means stop; do not go until green.

subject: DRV
body: A steady amber traffic light means
options: go if the way is clear
stop, unless you have crossed the stop line or are so close that stopping might cause a collision
explanation: Red follows amber.

subject: DRV
body: A green filter arrow at traffic lights means
options: give way to oncoming traffic only
you may go in that direction, even if the main light is red
explanation: Only move into that lane if you intend to go that way.

subject: DRV
body: A school crossing patrol shows a 'stop for children' sign. You must
options: slow down and drive past carefully
explanation: It is an offence not to stop.

subject: DRV
body: Someone supervising a learner driver must be at least
options: 21 years old and have held a full licence for that type of vehicle for 3 years
17 years old with a provisional licence
25 years old with a licence for 1 year
explanation: They must also be qualified to drive that type of vehicle.

subject: DRV
body: What is the minimum level of motor insurance required by law?
options: No insurance if the car is rarely used
explanation: It covers injury or damage to others.

subject: DRV
body: Who must you tell when you change your address?
explanation: Update your licence and vehicle log book (V5C).

subject: DRV
body: New drivers who get 6 or more penalty points within 2 years of passing their test will
options: have to pay a £100 fine only
have to take a theory test online only
explanation: They must reapply for a provisional licence and pass both tests again.

subject: DRV
body: Using a hand-held phone while driving can result in
options: no penalty if stopped at traffic lights
explanation: It is illegal even while stopped at lights or queuing.

subject: DRV
body: The UK car theory test multiple-choice part has 50 questions. What is the pass mark?
explanation: You have 57 minutes.

subject: DRV
body: In the hazard perception part of the theory test, how many video clips are there?
explanation: One clip has two developing hazards, so there are 15 to score; the pass mark is 44 out of 75.

subject: DRV
body: The legal drink-drive limit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland is
options: 80 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood
explanation: In Scotland it is 50 mg per 100 ml of blood.

subject: DRV
body: The legal drink-drive limit in Scotland is
options: 50 mg of alcohol per 100 ml of blood
explanation: The breath limit in Scotland is 22 micrograms per 100 ml.

subject: DRV
body: A car must have a valid MOT certificate (if one is required) before you can
explanation: Tax, MOT and insurance are all legal requirements.

subject: DRV
body: With a car (category B) licence, you can generally tow a trailer up to a maximum authorised mass of
explanation: Since 2021, car licence holders automatically have B+E entitlement.

subject: DRV
body: You are involved in a collision that damages another vehicle. You must
options: stop and give your name, address and registration to anyone with reasonable grounds to ask
leave a note and drive off
drive on if the damage is minor
explanation: If you cannot exchange details, report it to the police as soon as possible and within 24 hours.

subject: DRV
body: If you break down on a normal road, a warning triangle should be placed at least
explanation: Do not use a warning triangle on a motorway.

subject: DRV
body: At the scene of a crash, you should
options: switch off engines, warn other traffic and call emergency services
remove a motorcyclist's helmet straight away
explanation: Only move casualties if they are in further danger.

subject: DRV
body: An injured motorcyclist is lying unconscious. You should
options: not remove their helmet unless it is essential
explanation: Removing it could cause spinal injury.

subject: DRV
body: When are hazard warning lights used while moving?
options: Briefly on a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway to warn of a hazard ahead
explanation: Otherwise use them only when stationary and causing an obstruction.

subject: DRV
body: For CPR on an adult, the Highway Code advises chest compressions at a rate of
explanation: Press down 5–6 cm in the centre of the chest.

subject: DRV
body: A casualty has a burn. You should
options: cool it with clean, cool water for at least 10 minutes
remove clothing stuck to the burn
explanation: Do not remove anything stuck to the burn.

subject: DRV
body: If your vehicle catches fire, you should
options: get everyone out and away, then call the fire service
explanation: Do not attempt to tackle a large fire.

subject: DRV
body: You break down in a tunnel. You should
options: put a warning triangle in the next lane
switch on hazard lights, get out and call for help from an emergency point
stay in the car with the engine running
explanation: Follow the tunnel's emergency signs.

subject: DRV
body: A caravan starts to snake (swerve from side to side). You should
explanation: Let the speed fall gradually.

subject: DRV
body: When carrying a heavy load, you may need to
options: adjust your tyre pressures and headlight aim
explanation: Check the vehicle handbook.

subject: DRV
body: Who is responsible for making sure a vehicle is not overloaded?
options: The owner of the goods only
explanation: Overloading affects handling and braking.

subject: DRV
body: A roof rack load should be
options: securely fastened and not too heavy
explanation: Roof loads make the car less stable.

subject: DRV
body: Pets in a car should be
options: suitably restrained so they cannot distract you
in the boot of a saloon
explanation: A seat belt harness, carrier or dog guard is suitable.

subject: DRV
body: A car towing a caravan or trailer on a motorway has a speed limit of
explanation: It is 50 mph on single carriageways.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical overall stopping distance at 20 mph in good conditions?

subject: DRV

explanation: At 20 mph the thinking distance is 6 m.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical braking distance at 20 mph on a dry road?
explanation: At 20 mph the braking distance is 6 m.

subject: DRV

explanation: Thinking distance 9 m + braking distance 14 m = 23 m.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical thinking distance at 30 mph?
explanation: At 30 mph the thinking distance is 9 m.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical braking distance at 30 mph on a dry road?
explanation: At 30 mph the braking distance is 14 m.

subject: DRV

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical thinking distance at 40 mph?
explanation: At 40 mph the thinking distance is 12 m.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical braking distance at 40 mph on a dry road?
explanation: At 40 mph the braking distance is 24 m.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical overall stopping distance at 50 mph in good conditions?

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical thinking distance at 50 mph?
explanation: At 50 mph the thinking distance is 15 m.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical braking distance at 50 mph on a dry road?
explanation: At 50 mph the braking distance is 38 m.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical overall stopping distance at 60 mph in good conditions?
explanation: Thinking distance 18 m + braking distance 55 m = 73 m.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical thinking distance at 60 mph?
explanation: At 60 mph the thinking distance is 18 m.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical braking distance at 60 mph on a dry road?
explanation: At 60 mph the braking distance is 55 m.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical overall stopping distance at 70 mph in good conditions?
explanation: Thinking distance 21 m + braking distance 75 m = 96 m.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical thinking distance at 70 mph?
explanation: At 70 mph the thinking distance is 21 m.

subject: DRV
body: According to the Highway Code, what is the typical braking distance at 70 mph on a dry road?
explanation: At 70 mph the braking distance is 75 m.

subject: DRV
body: Unless signs show otherwise, what is the speed limit for a car on a built-up area with street lights (England)?
explanation: The limit for cars on a built-up area with street lights (England) is 30 mph.

subject: DRV
body: Unless signs show otherwise, what is the speed limit for a car towing a caravan or trailer on a built-up area with street lights (England)?
explanation: Cars towing are limited to 30 mph on a built-up area with street lights (England).

subject: DRV
body: Unless signs show otherwise, what is the speed limit for a car on a single carriageway?
explanation: The limit for cars on a single carriageway is 60 mph.

subject: DRV
body: Unless signs show otherwise, what is the speed limit for a car towing a caravan or trailer on a single carriageway?
explanation: Cars towing are limited to 50 mph on a single carriageway.

subject: DRV
body: Unless signs show otherwise, what is the speed limit for a car on a dual carriageway?
explanation: The limit for cars on a dual carriageway is 70 mph.

subject: DRV
body: Unless signs show otherwise, what is the speed limit for a car towing a caravan or trailer on a dual carriageway?
explanation: Cars towing are limited to 60 mph on a dual carriageway.

subject: DRV
body: Unless signs show otherwise, what is the speed limit for a car on a motorway?
explanation: The limit for cars on a motorway is 70 mph.

subject: DRV
body: Unless signs show otherwise, what is the speed limit for a car towing a caravan or trailer on a motorway?
explanation: Cars towing are limited to 60 mph on a motorway.

subject: DRV
body: The typical stopping distance at 30 mph is 23 m in the dry. Roughly how far could it be on a wet road?
explanation: Stopping distances at least double in the wet: 23 × 2 ≈ 46 m.

subject: DRV
body: The typical stopping distance at 50 mph is 53 m in the dry. Roughly how far could it be on a wet road?
explanation: Stopping distances at least double in the wet: 53 × 2 ≈ 106 m.

subject: DRV
body: The typical stopping distance at 70 mph is 96 m in the dry. Roughly how far could it be on a wet road?
explanation: Stopping distances at least double in the wet: 96 × 2 ≈ 192 m.

subject: DRV
body: The typical stopping distance at 60 mph is 73 m in the dry. Roughly how far could it be on a wet road?
explanation: Stopping distances at least double in the wet: 73 × 2 ≈ 146 m.

subject: DRV
body: The typical stopping distance at 40 mph is 36 m in the dry. Roughly how far could it be on a wet road?
explanation: Stopping distances at least double in the wet: 36 × 2 ≈ 72 m.

subject: DRV
body: The typical stopping distance at 20 mph is 12 m in the dry. Roughly how far could it be on a wet road?
explanation: Stopping distances at least double in the wet: 12 × 2 ≈ 24 m.

subject: DRV
body: When turning right at a crossroads where an oncoming vehicle is also turning right, the Highway Code's usual method is to
options: wait until the junction is completely empty every time
turn in front of it as fast as possible
pass offside to offside (keep the other vehicle on your right)
pass nearside to nearside without looking
explanation: Road layout or markings may make nearside to nearside necessary; check for oncoming traffic.

subject: DRV
body: On a two-lane dual carriageway, you should normally drive in
options: the left-hand lane, using the right-hand lane for overtaking or turning right
explanation: Return to the left lane when it is safe.

subject: DRV
body: At an unmarked crossroads, who has priority?
explanation: Treat it with great care and be ready to give way.

subject: DRV
body: At a 'stop' sign with a solid white line, you must
options: stop at the line even if the road looks clear
slow down and go if clear
explanation: Then go when it is safe.

subject: DRV
body: You are waiting to turn right from a main road into a side road. Where should you position your car?
options: Just left of the centre of the road
explanation: This lets traffic pass on your left.

subject: DRV
body: On a mini-roundabout, you should
options: give way to traffic from the right and avoid driving over the central marking if possible
give priority to traffic from the left
explanation: Large vehicles may have to drive over it.

subject: DRV
body: Where is the safest place to overtake a cyclist?
options: On a straight, clear road where you can leave at least 1.5 m
explanation: Wait behind if you can't pass safely.

subject: DRV
body: A one-way street has two lanes. To turn right at the end, you should normally use
explanation: Choose your lane early.

subject: DRV
body: When may you overtake on the left?
options: On a motorway whenever you want
When the vehicle ahead is signalling to turn right and there is room
explanation: Also in slow-moving queues where the left lane moves faster.

subject: DRV
body: When should you use the right-hand lane of a three-lane motorway?
options: For leaving at the next exit
explanation: Return to the left when you have passed.

subject: DRV
body: You should use dipped headlights during the day when
options: you are in a 20 mph zone
explanation: Make sure others can see you.

subject: DRV
body: A police officer in a car behind you flashes headlights and points to the left. You should
options: turn left at the next junction
pull up on the left when it is safe
explanation: Stop safely as soon as you can.

subject: DRV
body: An arm signal moved up and down from the driver's window means
options: I intend to slow down or stop
explanation: Arm signals can back up indicators.

subject: DRV
body: You should signal
options: only when another car is very close
to let other road users know your intentions, in good time
explanation: Cancel the signal afterwards.

subject: DRV
body: Emergency vehicles approach with blue lights. You should
options: help them pass, without breaking the law or putting others at risk
brake sharply in the middle of a junction
explanation: Stay calm and look for a safe place to pull over.

subject: DRV
body: Where must you NOT park?
options: On the zigzag lines of a pedestrian crossing
explanation: Other places include near the brow of a hill and opposite a junction.

subject: DRV
body: When parking on a hill facing downhill with a kerb, you should
options: turn the wheels away from the kerb
turn the wheels towards the kerb and apply the parking brake
explanation: If the brake fails, the kerb stops the car.

subject: DRV
body: Before you get out of a parked car, you should
options: check for cyclists and other traffic before opening the door
explanation: The 'Dutch reach' helps.

subject: DRV
body: At night, you must not park on a road facing
explanation: Your rear reflectors must face oncoming traffic.

subject: DRV
body: A white line across the road at a junction with 'Give Way' markings (broken double white lines) means
options: give way to traffic on the major road
explanation: An inverted triangle may also be painted on the road.

subject: DRV
body: A long white line with short gaps in the centre of the road is a
explanation: Do not cross it unless you can see the road is clear well ahead.

subject: DRV
body: A sign showing a red circle with a white horizontal bar means
explanation: Do not enter from this direction.

subject: DRV
body: A blue circle with a white arrow pointing left means
explanation: Blue circles give mandatory instructions.

subject: DRV
body: A rectangular blue sign with a white arrow pointing up shows
explanation: Blue rectangles give information.

subject: DRV
body: Red and white chevron signs on a bend show
options: a sharp deviation of the route
explanation: Slow down before the bend.

subject: DRV
body: A sign with a red border triangle showing a children symbol warns of
options: a school or area where children may be crossing
explanation: Slow down and be ready to stop.

subject: DRV
body: A triangular warning sign showing a gate before a railway symbol means
options: a level crossing without a barrier
a level crossing with a barrier or gate ahead
explanation: A steam-train symbol shows a crossing without a barrier.

subject: DRV
body: Yellow lines painted across the road (rumble or 'yellow bar' markings) on the approach to a roundabout are there to
options: make you aware of your speed
explanation: They encourage you to slow down.

subject: DRV
body: Traffic lights showing red and amber together mean
options: stop — do not go until green shows
go if the junction is clear
explanation: Green comes next.

subject: DRV
body: Flashing red lights at a fire station, level crossing or swing bridge mean
explanation: Wait until they stop flashing.

subject: DRV
body: Which of these must NOT use a motorway?
explanation: Also pedestrians, cyclists, horse riders and slow vehicles.

subject: DRV
body: Flashing amber lights on a motorway gantry warn of
options: a hazard ahead — the speed limit shown may be lower
explanation: Adjust your speed and look out for the hazard.

subject: DRV
body: On a smart motorway, emergency areas are marked with
options: orange signs and an orange surface
explanation: They have an SOS phone.

subject: DRV
body: If you break down on a motorway hard shoulder, you should
options: try to repair it in the lane
get out on the passenger side and wait behind the barrier if safe
explanation: Leave animals in the car unless in an emergency.

subject: DRV
body: Driving in heavy motorway traffic, you notice a ramp meter (traffic lights) on the slip road. They are there to
options: control the flow of traffic joining the motorway
explanation: Wait for green.

subject: DRV
body: Why should you leave a large gap from the vehicle in front on a motorway?
options: To have enough time to react and stop safely at high speed
explanation: Use the two-second rule.

subject: DRV
body: When driving at night, you should
options: drive with lights off in towns
use dipped headlights if dazzling other road users with full beam
explanation: Dip your lights for oncoming and preceding traffic.

subject: DRV
body: If you are dazzled by oncoming headlights at night, you should
explanation: Never retaliate with full beam.

subject: DRV
body: On a wet road where aquaplaning is a risk, the safest thing to do beforehand is
options: increase speed to get through water
explanation: Slower speeds reduce aquaplaning risk.

subject: DRV
body: In icy conditions, the steering feels very light. This probably means
options: the tyres have lost grip on ice
explanation: Ease off and avoid sudden movements.

subject: DRV
body: When driving through deep water, you should
options: drive slowly in a low gear
drive fast to create a bow wave
explanation: Test your brakes afterwards.

subject: DRV
body: When following another vehicle in fog, you should
options: keep a safe distance and be able to stop within the distance you can see
explanation: Slow down; fog can thicken quickly.

subject: DRV
body: Your windscreen mists up. You should
options: wipe a small hole and drive
use the demister and wait until it is clear before driving
drive with the window down only
explanation: You must be able to see clearly through all windows.

subject: DRV
body: You are driving past a line of parked cars and see a ball bounce between them. What hazard should you expect?
explanation: Slow down and be ready to stop.

subject: DRV
body: Driving near a school at going-home time, you should
options: sound your horn as you pass
slow down and watch for children and parked cars
explanation: Children may be distracted.

subject: DRV
body: A car ahead is driving erratically and drifting across the lane. You should
options: stay well back and report it to the police if necessary
explanation: The driver may be ill, tired or impaired.

subject: DRV
body: Approaching a narrow bridge with traffic lights, the lights are red. You should
options: go if no traffic is coming
explanation: The bridge may only allow one-way traffic.

subject: DRV
body: Which is most likely to make you tired while driving?
options: A short journey in the morning
A long journey in a warm car at night
explanation: Plan breaks and stop if tired.

subject: DRV
body: Why should you avoid sudden braking on a downhill road?
options: You could lose control and skid
explanation: Brake gently and early.

subject: DRV
body: When should you take extra care for motorcyclists?
options: At junctions and when changing lanes
explanation: Look twice for bikes.

subject: DRV
body: A horse rider is in the left lane approaching a roundabout and signalling right. You should
options: be prepared for them to stay in the left lane and keep well back
explanation: Horse riders often keep left at roundabouts.

subject: DRV
body: Before turning left across a cycle lane, you should
options: check for cyclists on your left and give way to them
explanation: Do not cut across cyclists going straight ahead.

subject: DRV
body: Why should you be cautious near an animal-drawn vehicle or a flock of sheep?
options: They have right of way only at night
explanation: Drive slowly and do not sound your horn.

subject: DRV
body: You see a person with a guide dog at the kerb. You should
options: sound your horn to warn them
be ready to stop — they may intend to cross
explanation: Be patient and give them time.

subject: DRV
body: Driving with under-inflated tyres can
options: increase fuel consumption and reduce grip
explanation: Check pressures regularly.

subject: DRV
body: Your vehicle pulls to one side when braking. This is likely to be
explanation: Have it checked as soon as possible.

subject: DRV
body: Which lights must work on your car?
options: All required lights, including headlights, brake lights and indicators
Only lights you use at night
explanation: Check them regularly.

subject: DRV
body: Why is it dangerous to leave items loose on a parcel shelf?
options: They could fly forward and injure someone in a sudden stop
explanation: Secure loose items.

subject: DRV
body: Before a long journey, which checks should you make?
options: Fuel, oil, water, tyres and lights
None if the car is new
explanation: Remember the acronym POWDER: petrol, oil, water, damage, electrics, rubber.

subject: DRV
body: Who is responsible for making sure a vehicle is roadworthy?
options: The garage that last serviced it
explanation: Drivers can be prosecuted for unroadworthy vehicles.

subject: DRV
body: Which document shows who is the registered keeper of a vehicle?
explanation: Keep it up to date.

subject: DRV
body: How long must a learner driver hold a provisional licence before taking the practical test?
options: There is no minimum time — they must first pass the theory test
explanation: The theory test pass is valid for 2 years.

subject: DRV
body: A theory test pass certificate is valid for
explanation: You must pass the practical test within this time.

subject: DRV
body: Driving without insurance can lead to
options: an unlimited fine, penalty points and the vehicle being seized
explanation: It is also unfair on other road users.

subject: DRV
body: Your car fails its MOT on a dangerous fault. You
options: must not drive it until the fault is repaired
can drive it until your old MOT expires
can drive it if you go slowly
explanation: Dangerous faults make the vehicle illegal to drive.

subject: DRV
body: At the scene of an incident, an injured person is not breathing. You should
explanation: Use an AED if one is available.

subject: DRV
body: A casualty is bleeding heavily from a leg. You should
options: apply firm pressure to the wound
explanation: Raise the limb if no bones are broken.

subject: DRV
body: A casualty is in shock. You should
options: keep them warm, reassure them and not give them anything to drink
explanation: Call for help.

subject: DRV
body: Your car breaks down on a level crossing and a train is coming. You should
options: get everyone out and away immediately
stay inside with seat belts on
explanation: Move well clear of the crossing.

subject: DRV
body: If a tyre bursts while driving, you should
options: hold the steering wheel firmly and let the car slow down gradually
explanation: Stop in a safe place.
